propositions.text: This judicial review application relates to the RAD decision upholding the RPD's rejection of the refugee claim under sections 96 and 97 of the Act.
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review is related to the decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) which, on April 5, 2019, upheld the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting the refugee protection claim made under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [the Act].

propositions.text: The only issue is whether the applicant's fear due to religious beliefs in Algeria was credible.
propositions.quote: The only issue in this case is whether the applicant’s fear due to his religious beliefs in his country of origin, Algeria, was credible.

propositions.text: Neither the RPD nor the RAD believed the applicant's claim.
propositions.quote: Neither the RPD nor the RAD believed the applicant.

propositions.text: The applicant failed to convince the Court that the RAD's decision was unreasonable; the judicial review application must be dismissed.
propositions.quote: He did not succeed in doing so, and the application for judicial review must be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the judicial review concerns the RAD decision upholding the RPD's rejection of the refugee claim; the issue is credibility of fear; both divisions disbelieved the applicant; the review is dismissed.

propositions.text: Mr. Bouarif is an Algerian who converted gradually to Christianity starting in 2009.
propositions.quote: Mr. Bouarif is a resident of Algeria who stated that he gradually converted to Christianity starting in 2009.

propositions.text: From 2009 to 2014, conflicts over his religious practice were minor and not serious.
propositions.quote: From his testimony, we note that from 2009 to 2014, there were only minor conflicts over his emerging religious practice, which he himself stated were not serious.

propositions.text: November 2014 was the tipping point when conflicts became more difficult.
propositions.quote: It appears that November 2014 was the tipping point when lively discussions evolved into to a more difficult situation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant converted to Christianity starting 2009; minor conflicts occurred until November 2014, when difficulties increased.

propositions.text: The applicant did not claim difficulties caused by Islamists in his BOC Form but described attacks on a Christian meeting place in November and December 2014.
propositions.quote: Actually, the applicant did not even claim in his Basis of Claim (BOC) Form to have suffered the said difficulties caused by the Islamists, but rather that groups of young people attacked in November 2014, and specifically on November 15, 2014, the house of a person who apparently taught certain precepts of the Christian religion.

propositions.text: In December 2014, the same group ransacked the house and stole objects; the village committee excluded young Christians from social activities; authorities ordered closure of the house in January 2015.
propositions.quote: In December 2014, this same group reportedly came to the same house (the meeting place for prayer) where they ransacked everything and stole objects. Later in 2014, the village committee reportedly decided to exclude young Christians from all the village’s social activities. Finally, in January 2015, the authorities reportedly ordered the closure of the house.

propositions.text: The group then went to a large church in Ouadhia city.
propositions.quote: It was then that the group went to a large church in the city of Ouadhia.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant did not claim Islamist difficulties in his BOC Form but described attacks on a Christian house and exclusion from social activities in late 2014.

propositions.text: The applicant decided to leave Algeria because he felt excluded and marginalized.
propositions.quote: It was when that the applicant decided to leave his country because he felt excluded there. The applicant repeatedly stated during the hearing before the RPD that he was marginalized in his country.

propositions.text: The applicant stated his intention was to stay in Canada and seek asylum because he was oppressed in Algeria.
propositions.quote: he stated on page 32 of 110 that [translation] “[m]y intention was to come here and stay here, and possibly ask the authorities here for their protection, asylum so that I could stay here because I was oppressed in my country”.

propositions.text: The administrative tribunals found the applicant was neither a refugee nor a person in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Act.
propositions.quote: The administrative tribunals found that the applicant was neither a refugee nor a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the applicant left Algeria feeling marginalized and oppressed, intending to seek asylum; tribunals found he was not a refugee or protected person.

propositions.text: The only decision before the Court is the RAD decision, which follows the RPD's decision on the applicant's lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The only decision before this Court is the RAD decision. Essentially, the RAD follows the RPD’s decision regarding the applicant’s lack of credibility.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim for reasons including vague prepared testimony, poor knowledge of Christianity, omission of a personal incident, and delay in applying for refugee protection.
propositions.quote: In paragraph 13 of its decision, the RAD reiterated the reasons why the RPD denied the refugee claim given the applicant’s credibility: [translation] [13] In its decision, the RPD rejected the appellant’s claim for the following reasons: - The appellant gave a prepared and vague testimony regarding the problems he had allegedly experienced in Algeria; - His testimony was vague as regards his knowledge of the Christian religion, testifying to a quasi-ignorance of it; - The appellant testified during his testimony to a personal incident that took place in November 2014 where Islamists allegedly wanted to attack him physically, but he never mentioned it on his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form); - The behaviour of the appellant, who took six months to apply for refugee protection once in Canada, is not that of a person fearful of returning to his country of origin.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the RAD decision follows the RPD's rejection of the claim due to the applicant's vague testimony, poor religious knowledge, omission of a personal incident, and delay in applying.

propositions.text: The RAD found the applicant's knowledge of Christianity was meager and erroneous, undermining his credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the applicant’s knowledge of the religion he claimed to practise was meager, even erroneous (RAD Decision, para 26).

propositions.text: The RAD's assessment that the applicant's poor religious knowledge was not an issue requiring expertise is agreed with by the Court.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the RAD, this is not an issue that requires expertise. One must agree.

propositions.text: The applicant confused Mary the mother of Christ as one of the twelve apostles and confused apostle and disciple.
propositions.quote: Besides Easter and Christmas, the applicant could not indicate any other religious holidays... it was rather striking that Mary, the mother of Christ, was presented as one of the twelve apostles... the applicant seemed to confuse apostle and disciple.

propositions.text: The applicant could not identify a prayer despite repeated questions, showing poor knowledge inconsistent with claimed religious participation.
propositions.quote: the applicant was unable to identify a prayer, as specifically asked, simply saying, despite repeated questions, that he prayed often.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found the applicant's religious knowledge poor and erroneous, including confusion about Mary and inability to identify prayers; the Court agrees this requires no expertise.

propositions.text: The RAD cited Gao v Canada that the Board may consider expected religious knowledge but should not impose unreasonably high standards or focus on minutiae.
propositions.quote: This can be a difficult task for the Board, as it is entitled to consider whether the claimant holds a level of religious knowledge that would be expected of someone in the claimant’s position but should not reach an adverse conclusion based on minutiae or holding the claimant to an unreasonably high standard of religious knowledge.

propositions.text: The RAD found the applicant's lack of basic religious knowledge justified a negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: Anyone who claims to have adhered to a religion for which he was allegedly persecuted in his country of origin should know the most basic elements.

propositions.text: The purpose of religious knowledge inquiry is to assess credibility, not to probe personal faith.
propositions.quote: The purpose is not to search hearts and minds, but rather to assess the credibility of the refugee claimant who claims to belong to a religion of which he does not know the basic precepts.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD cited Gao v Canada that basic religious knowledge is expected to assess credibility, not to probe personal faith, justifying negative inference for lack of knowledge.

propositions.text: The omission of a personal bullying incident from the BOC Form was significant and undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that... this event affecting the applicant personally is not indicated anywhere in his account... For the RPD, this was a significant omission.

propositions.text: The RAD also found the omission undermined credibility.
propositions.quote: The RAD also found that this omission undermined the applicant’s credibility (RAD Decision, para 44).

propositions.text: The six-month delay before applying for refugee status affected credibility regarding fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: The RAD noted that the wait of some six months before applying for refugee status in Canada affected the applicant’s credibility with respect to a fear of persecution in connection with the practice of Christianity.

propositions.text: The RAD considered the delay as one factor among others to dismiss the claim.
propositions.quote: [translation] “[t]he SPR did not err, it considered this point as one factor among others in order to dismiss the appellant’s request” (RAD decision, para 53).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the omission of a personal incident and six-month delay in applying undermined the applicant's credibility and supported dismissal.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the RAD's points have different meanings and does not show the decision was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeks to take up each of the points raised by the administrative tribunals and give them a different meaning. He does not demonstrate that the decision was unreasonable...

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness as confirmed by Vavilov, with no exceptions here.
propositions.quote: There is no doubt that the standard of review in this area is that of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov]).

propositions.text: The applicant alleges three errors: unreasonable analytical framework on religious questioning; factual errors; and unreasonable consideration of delay.
propositions.quote: Here, the applicant pointed out what he considered to be three errors that taint the reasonableness of the decision: (a) the analytical framework adopted was unreasonable and erroneous because it allowed questioning in religious matters; (b) determinative factual errors marred the decision; and (c) it was unreasonable to consider that the applicant’s delay in filing his refugee claim was inappropriate.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the RAD's points have different meanings and alleges errors in religious questioning, factual findings, and delay consideration; the court confirms reasonableness review.

propositions.text: The applicant claims the RAD imposed a 'biblical knowledge test' rather than examining faith authenticity.
propositions.quote: In the applicant’s view, the questions posed by the RAD were aimed at imposing [translation] “a biblical knowledge test” rather than examining the authenticity and genuineness of his faith.

propositions.text: A claimant persecuted for religious beliefs must be familiar with basic information about that religion; authenticity of beliefs can be assessed.
propositions.quote: he who says that he is persecuted because of his religious beliefs to the point of having to go into exile must be familiar with the basic information relating to this religious belief.

propositions.text: Li v Canada states the RPD can assess genuineness of religious belief and knowledge, relying on motive and sincerity to reject claims.
propositions.quote: It is well established in law that it is open to the RPD to assess and consider a refugee protection claimant’s motive for practising a religion, including the genuineness of those religious beliefs, and to rely on that motive in rejecting the refugee protection claim...

propositions.text: Findings of lack of credibility and fabricated stories about religion reasonably support conclusion of insincere religious beliefs.
propositions.quote: Findings that the claimant lacks credibility, that he or she has fabricated stories about practising the claimed religion... have been held by this Court to reasonably support a conclusion that the sincerity of the claimant’s religious beliefs is not genuine.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges a 'biblical knowledge test'; the court cites Li v Canada allowing RPD to assess religious knowledge and sincerity to reject claims.

propositions.text: The reviewing court must avoid substituting its opinion for the administrative decision-maker's expertise on religious belief genuineness.
propositions.quote: The Court, in judicial review, must avoid substituting its opinion for that of the administrative decision maker in whom responsibility has been entrusted by Parliament.

propositions.text: Hou v Canada states assessing genuineness of religious beliefs is difficult and delegated to the Board; courts should defer absent disregard or misapprehension.
propositions.quote: assessing the genuineness of the claimant’s religious beliefs is a difficult task and “this challenging job has been delegated to the Board as the finder of fact and this Court cannot, on judicial review, decide to, in effect, reweigh the results of what can look like a round of Bible trivia”

propositions.text: Wang states vague or lacking detail testimony can justify rejecting claims as non-credible; courts should defer to Board's expertise.
propositions.quote: Testimony lacking in detail that would reasonably be expected of a person in the claimant’s position is a basis for rejecting claims as non-credible even if the Applicant was able to answer some other questions, and with great detail.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Hou and Wang emphasizing deference to administrative expertise in assessing religious belief genuineness and credibility.

propositions.text: The applicant's inability to answer basic religious questions and baptism timing supports RAD's conclusion of lack of genuine religious practice.
propositions.quote: not being able to answer such basic questions... clearly illustrates that the RAD had before it evidence on which to base its conclusion that the applicant did not demonstrate the genuineness of his religious practice.

propositions.text: The RAD's finding on religious knowledge is reasonable and not a microscopic or probing analysis.
propositions.quote: This finding is reasonable. We are nowhere near asking questions that are probing and that stem from a microscopic analysis of an area as sensitive as religious identification.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant's poor religious knowledge supports the RAD's reasonable conclusion of insincere religious practice, not microscopic probing.

propositions.text: The applicant's reference to Mary was ambiguous and likely meant Mary the mother of Christ, not Mary Magdalene; this does not change the RAD's conclusion.
propositions.quote: It seems clear to me that when the applicant referred to Mary, he meant to refer to the mother of Christ... In my opinion, this does not change the conclusion reached by the RAD.

propositions.text: The applicant's knowledge of religion based on a vague film recollection is astonishing for a claimed adherent.
propositions.quote: In fact, the knowledge of a religion based on a vague recollection of a film is in itself astonishing for one who claims to be of this religion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant's ambiguous reference to Mary and reliance on a film do not alter the RAD's conclusion on his poor religious knowledge.

propositions.text: Omission of a significant personal violent incident from the BOC Form is a valid basis for negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: The omission in the BOC Form of a close call with a violent confrontation is also significant... The only one that implicated him was that of November 2014, and he did not mention it in his BOC Form.

propositions.text: Prior cases confirm important facts must appear in PIF; omissions can affect credibility and justify negative inferences.
propositions.quote: This Court has confirmed on a number of occasions that all the important facts of a claim must appear in the PIF and that failing to mention them could affect the credibility of part or all of the testimony.

propositions.text: Adding important facts later can be seen as embellishment and affect credibility negatively.
propositions.quote: The effect of adding to the story is obvious. It is an attempt to embellish the story to include a more personal element to personalize the persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds omission of a personal violent incident from the BOC Form significant and cites prior cases supporting negative credibility inferences for such omissions.

propositions.text: Delay in claiming refugee protection is puzzling but not determinative; it is one factor among others affecting credibility.
propositions.quote: The failure to claim refugee protection soon after his arrival in Canada is also puzzling, even if this fact is not determinative of the issues and its relative weight is not significant.

propositions.text: Delay in seeking asylum can indicate lack of genuine fear, as recognized in prior Federal Court cases.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal has recognized that the fact that a person does not seek asylum at the first opportunity is a factor that indicates that the person does not have a genuine subjective fear.

propositions.text: The Board can impugn credibility based on delay and failure to claim at first opportunity; explanations must be reasonable.
propositions.quote: The Board was entitled to impugn the applicants’ credibility based on the applicants’ delay in claiming refugee status, and their failure to claim at the first opportunity... This is not an explanation that justifies the applicants’ failure to claim in the numerous safe countries they travelled through.

propositions.text: Vavilov confirms reasonableness standard and deference to administrative expertise in decision-making.
propositions.quote: In its decision in Vavilov, the Court did not abandon the deference owed to an administrative tribunal, but rather announced that the analysis should henceforth be centered on the reasonableness of the decision...

propositions.text: The RAD's decision is reasonable and benefits from deference despite puzzling delay.
propositions.quote: Benefitting from the deference of the Court, I have come to the conclusion that the RAD’s decision...

paragraphs.summary: The court finds delay in claiming refugee protection puzzling but not determinative; prior cases and Vavilov support considering delay as one factor; RAD's decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires understanding the decision maker's reasoning for justification, transparency, and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: A reviewing court must develop an understanding of the decision maker’s reasoning process in order to determine whether the hallmarks of a reasonable decision are present—justification, transparency and intelligibility...

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness review requires assessing justification, transparency, and intelligibility of the decision maker's reasoning.

propositions.text: Vavilov confirms the high threshold for unreasonableness; minor flaws do not justify overturning decisions.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the party challenging the decision to show that it is unreasonable... Any alleged flaws or shortcomings must be more than merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision.

propositions.text: Only serious shortcomings central to the decision can render it unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the court must be satisfied that any shortcomings or flaws relied on by the party challenging the decision are sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Vavilov's high threshold for unreasonableness requires serious, central shortcomings to overturn decisions, not minor flaws.

propositions.text: The applicant argues the RPD erred examining the baptismal certificate and the RAD failed to correct this error.
propositions.quote: The applicant made much of the error allegedly made by the RPD when it examined the baptismal certificate presented by the applicant. Since the RPD’s decision is not before this Court, the applicant therefore complained that the RAD did not correct the error.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges the RPD erred on the baptismal certificate and the RAD failed to correct this error.

propositions.text: The RPD was mistaken in seeing a typing or spelling error on the baptismal certificate; it was a misleading font.
propositions.quote: It is clear that the RPD was mistaken in seeing a typing error or a spelling error when there was none on the baptismal certificate presented in evidence before the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD mistakenly saw a typing or spelling error on the baptismal certificate due to font.

propositions.text: The RAD did not rely on the RPD's baptismal certificate error and did not need to correct it; the error was peripheral and had no bearing on the decision.
propositions.quote: The RAD made no mention of it since the RAD did not rely on what was obviously an RPD error... The RPD’s error had no bearing on its decision.

propositions.text: The complaint that the RAD did not report the RPD error is superficial and does not warrant judicial review.
propositions.quote: The complaint made to the RAD for not having reported the error has no bearing. There are no “serious shortcomings”. If there was a shortcoming, it would have only been superficial and incidental.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD did not rely on the RPD's baptismal certificate error; the error was peripheral and the complaint is superficial, not warranting review.

propositions.text: The RAD’s decision was reasonable, justified, transparent and intelligible.
propositions.quote: The Court therefore concludes that the RAD’s decision was reasonable in that it was justified, transparent and intelligible.

propositions.text: No question to be certified under section 74 of the Act, as parties agree.
propositions.quote: There is no question to be certified under section 74 of the Act, as the parties agree.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed;

propositions.text: No serious question of general importance is certified.
propositions.quote: No serious question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the RAD decision was reasonable and dismisses the judicial review application; no question is certified under section 74, as parties agree.
